title: Fundamental theorem of calculus, part I, for a uniformly continuous integrand
statement: THE FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF CALCULUS, PART I, in the form a textbook states it. For F uniformly continuous on the closed interval [a, b] of the constructive reals, the function G(x) = the integral of F from a to the clamped x has derivative F on [a, b], in Bishop's UNIFORM sense: CReal.HasDerivativeOn carries an explicit modulus as a data field, not an existential, and the modulus here is E |-> (modulus of uniform continuity of F)(2E + 1) -- two halves of 1/(2E+2) summing to the 1/(E+1) the specification asks for. NO side condition beyond uniform continuity: the (kb : Nat) and BoundedOn F a b kb that CReal.hasDerivative_antiderivative demands of its caller are discharged here from the uniform-continuity witness, because CReal.bounded_of_uniformly_continuous COMPUTES such a kb (one Nat expression in F, a, b, u) with no Exists-elimination. Nothing about the estimate is re-proved: the proof term IS that theorem applied.

formal.statement: theorem CReal.hasDerivative_antiderivative_of_uc : ((x0 : ((x0 : CReal) -> CReal)) -> ((x1 : CReal) -> ((x2 : CReal) -> ((x3 : CReal.le x1 x2) -> ((x4 : CReal.UniformlyContinuousOn x0 x1 x2) -> CReal.HasDerivativeOn (CReal.antiderivative x0 x1 x2 x3 x4) x0 x1 x2)))))

notes:
WHAT THIS ADDS, PRECISELY. CReal.hasDerivative_antiderivative (landed 2026-08-27) already proves FTC-I; this fact is not a new theorem about the reals but a STRENGTHENING OF ITS STATEMENT, from arity 7 to arity 5, by discharging a hypothesis that was always derivable. A reader who wants 'the fundamental theorem of calculus' can apply this one without first constructing a magnitude bound.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY. It is not a two-sided derivative in the classical punctured-limit sense; CReal.HasDerivativeOn's spec quantifies over an UNORDERED pair x, y in [a, b] with |y - x| inside the modulus, which is the uniform (Bishop) notion and is STRONGER than pointwise differentiability. It says nothing off [a, b]. The integrand's uniform continuity is not a convenience: on a constructive line CReal.le is undecidable, so 'sup over partitions' is unavailable and a merely pointwise-continuous function cannot be integrated by this route at all.

WHY THE BOUND WAS THERE AT ALL. CReal.hasDerivative_antiderivative routes through CReal.integral_abs_le_of_bound, which needs a magnitude bound on F. Taking it as a hypothesis was the cheaper thing to do at the time; discharging it costs one application of CReal.bounded_of_uniformly_continuous and a K read back off the INFERRED type of that application -- never hand-derived, because the computed K is rescale_index(3, modulus F a b u 0)-shaped and rebuilding it would force a full unfold.
